record.original_question: Given a Diophantine equation, either list all its integer solutions or prove that it has infinitely many integer solutions.

evidence.quote: We next consider the following more restricted but completely rigorous question.
Problem 4. Given a Diophantine equation, either list all its integer solutions, or prove that there are infinitely many of them.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Design an algorithm (or establish the impossibility of one) which, given as input an arbitrary polynomial Diophantine equation P(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) = 0 with integer coefficients, produces one of the following two correct outputs:

(a) a finite, complete list of all integer tuples (x_1, ..., x_n) ∈ Z^n satisfying P(x_1, ..., x_n) = 0, in the case that the solution set is finite; or

(b) a rigorous mathematical proof that the equation has infinitely many integer solutions, in the case that the solution set is infinite.

Equivalently, determine whether for every polynomial P ∈ Z[x_1, ..., x_n] one of the two tasks above can be carried out, and if so, exhibit a uniform method.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a weakened variant of Hilbert's tenth problem restricted to a finiteness dichotomy. Hilbert's tenth problem over Z was shown undecidable by Matiyasevich (1970), but the specific question of algorithmically distinguishing finitely-many-solutions vs infinitely-many-solutions cases (and listing solutions in the finite case) is generally regarded as open; no known algorithm achieves this in general, and there is no known undecidability proof for this restricted version.

status_evidence.title: Hilbert's tenth problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Matiyasevich's theorem implies that there is no algorithm which can decide whether a Diophantine equation has any solutions in integers.
status_evidence.claim: The full decision problem is undecidable, but the finite/infinite dichotomy variant is not known to be decidable or undecidable.
